searchText: I have written a description of the EIP-1559 txpool for fast sorting. Please let me know if there are any unclear points :) https://hackmd.io/@VVsmryteTEWuiOBecRGFhw/Hy0ZyFn3w (https://ethereum-magicians.org/t/eip-1559-transaction-pool-for-fast-sorting/5051) <@!370136219927052298> For the tree keys, you want first-seen-time as the secondary sort term, then `transaction_hash` as the final sort term. Geth used to use `transaction_hash` as its secondary and this lead to some very bad behaviors as bots tried to back-run transactions (guarantee ordering immediately after a target transaction). <@!370136219927052298> For the vector column, you have `Add a transaction` as an `O(1)` cost, but presumably when using a vector one is adding in sort order (not just to the end), which is not `O(1)`. That is, I don't think anyone uses a raw vector for transactions, it is *always* a sorted vector. > `k` is small if the change of basefee is small. I believe this should be: > `k` is small if the change of basefee results in few transactions becoming capped by `fee_cap`. Whether this true or not depends heavily on how much people are over-allocating to fee_cap. One can imagine a world where the fee cap is quite low (e.g., 1 nanoeth) and people are regularly setting their `fee_cap` to 50 nanoeth. In such a world even when the `basefee` moves the maximal distance per block, it still wouldn't cause a large number of transactions to jump pools. IIUC, this strategy essentially sacrifices memory in exchange for speed by keeping 3 separate indexes into the data? Though, the memory costs may be inconsequential if your SBST data structure is reasonably efficient. Thank you for the response! > For the vector column, you have Add a transaction as an O(1) cost, but presumably when using a vector one is adding in sort order (not just to the end), which is not O(1). I don't know the implementation of Geth, but does it sort each time a transaction is added? I think that would be inefficient and it would be sorted in batch (for instance, when producing a block). I have never looked, but I always imagined that the transactions were in a linked list and when one is added it was added in sort order. Rather than re-sorting the whole thing every block. It may be worth mentioning in this document dropping the least profitable transaction. I believe that finding least profitable is effectively the same cost as finding the most profitable? > I have never looked, but I always imagined that the transactions were in a linked list and when one is added it was added in sort order. If we use a linked list, we can add and delete in O(log n) using a binary search, but if we use a vector, it is O(n). > I believe that finding least profitable is effectively the same cost as finding the most profitable? Yes! This can runs in O(log n). On a related topic, I do have to wonder if the simplest solution here is to target smaller mempools and just re-sort the whole thing after each run. If your mempool is only 1000 items large, re-calculated the sort the index after every block may be sufficiently cheap that any additional complexity isn't worth it. Perhaps there is a reason we want very large mempools though, in which case your proposal seems quite reasonable. > IIUC, this strategy essentially sacrifices memory in exchange for speed by keeping 3 separate indexes into the data? > Though, the memory costs may be inconsequential if your SBST data structure is reasonably efficient. The space complexity is the same, but it is constant times less memory efficient. Since we have to prepare three SBSTs, we need to keep three times the transaction metadata (fee_cap, max_miner_brbe, hash, etc). > On a related topic, I do have to wonder if the simplest solution here is to target smaller mempools and just re-sort the whole thing after each run. If your mempool is only 1000 items large, re-calculated the sort the index after every block may be sufficiently cheap that any additional complexity isn't worth it. That's right. I think that if there are only 1000 transactions, the vector implementation is fine. For at least 10,000 txs, we can see the speed advantage. I was told that the default value for the number of transactions held in Geth is 8192. I question the reasonableness of the current Geth default. 😄 But that is a separate conversation. 😉 > If we use a linked list, we can add and delete in O(log n) using a binary search Correction: A linked list cannot runs a binary search in O(log n). Addition and deletion in a linked list runs in O(n). this is probably a bad assumption to make, but assuming `(base_fee + tip) < next_base_fee`, you could theoretically use a linked list of linked lists to significantly increase performance of all operations with little memory overhead since you could ignore all other transactions that don't have the same `base_fee` ``` ^ | base_fee 3 -> tip1 -> tip2 -> tip3 | base_fee 2 -> tip1 | base_fee 1 -> tip1 -> tip2 -> tip3 -> tip4 -> tip5 ``` now this goes completely out the window if `base_fee 2 + tip1 > base_fee3` although it wouldn't be impossible to "promote" these transactions when a new `base fee` is generated 🤔

excerpts.content: <@!370136219927052298> For the tree keys, you want first-seen-time as the secondary sort term, then `transaction_hash` as the final sort term.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: Geth used to use `transaction_hash` as its secondary and this lead to some very bad behaviors as bots tried to back-run transactions (guarantee ordering immediately after a target transaction).

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: <@!370136219927052298> For the vector column, you have `Add a transaction` as an `O(1)` cost, but presumably when using a vector one is adding in sort order (not just to the end), which is not `O(1)`.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: That is, I don't think anyone uses a raw vector for transactions, it is *always* a sorted vector.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content:
> `k` is small if the change of basefee is small.
I believe this should be:
> `k` is small if the change of basefee results in few transactions becoming capped by `fee_cap`.
Whether this true or not depends heavily on how much people are over-allocating to fee_cap.  One can imagine a world where the fee cap is quite low (e.g., 1 nanoeth) and people are regularly setting their `fee_cap` to 50 nanoeth.  In such a world even when the `basefee` moves the maximal distance per block, it still wouldn't cause a large number of transactions to jump pools.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: Though, the memory costs may be inconsequential if your SBST data structure is reasonably efficient.

excerpts.author: minaminao
excerpts.content:
> I have never looked, but I always imagined that the transactions were in a linked list and when one is added it was added in sort order.
If we use a linked list, we can add and delete in O(log n) using a binary search, but if we use a vector, it is O(n).

> I believe that finding least profitable is effectively the same cost as finding the most profitable?
Yes! This can runs in O(log n).

If your mempool is only 1000 items large, re-calculated the sort the index after every block may be sufficiently cheap that any additional complexity isn't worth it.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus

Since we have to prepare three SBSTs, we need to keep three times the transaction metadata (fee_cap, max_miner_brbe, hash, etc).
